query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A single-phase face‐centered cubic (FCC) high-entropy alloy, such as the equiatomic CoNiCrFeMn (Cantor alloy), exhibits exceptional ductility at ambient conditions because its homogeneous microstructure activates multiple slip systems and supports favorable dislocation dynamics.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoNiCrFeMn) at room temperature and atmospheric pressure.
generation.intervention: Perform combined in situ tensile testing and atomistic simulations to monitor dislocation activity and slip system engagement during deformation.
generation.conditions: Room temperature, ambient pressure, and standard strain rate tensile loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniform distribution of alloying elements and the resulting activation of multiple slip systems that facilitate homogeneous dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: The high number of available slip systems in the FCC structure allows for extensive plastic deformation through the coordinated motion of dislocations, yielding high ductility while maintaining strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Experimental tensile tests will show a high strain-to-failure, and atomistic simulations will reveal extensive slip system activation and uniform dislocation dynamics correlating with the observed ductility.
generation.baseline: Traditional FCC ductile metals (e.g., copper or aluminum) which are ductile but may not display the same strength–ductility synergy as FCC high-entropy alloys.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under ambient conditions and for alloys maintaining a single-phase FCC structure; significant deviations in temperature, strain rate, or the introduction of secondary phases could alter the ductility mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative role of multiple slip systems is supported, the quantitative relationship between specific dislocation dynamics and ductility in HEAs requires further calibration and may vary with compositional and microstructural nuances.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of in situ tensile tests on CoNiCrFeMn alloy specimens while simultaneously performing atomistic simulations to capture real-time dislocation movement and slip system activity. Compare the fracture strains, deformation uniformity, and slip band patterns with those predicted by the simulations.
measurements: Tensile stress-strain curves to determine strain-to-failure.
TEM imaging to capture active dislocation dynamics and slip band formation.
Simulation output quantifying slip system activation and dislocation mobility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tensile tests do not show enhanced ductility compared to conventional FCC metals or if the atomistic simulations fail to confirm the predicted widespread and coordinated slip system activity, then the hypothesis that the ductility arises from the FCC structure's multiple slip systems is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] . High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures.
